newsitem.title: USA: YEAR - Wall Street faces tough 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAR - Wall Street faces tough 1997.

text.p: Storm clouds are gathering over Wall Street and may erupt into the stiffest correction in years during 1997 as slower corporate earnings growth and greater market volatility encumber the aging bull market.

While a few analysts expect a downright bear market of the 20 percent-plus magnitude, most of Wall Street's crystal ball gazers see a more shallow pullback and a return to the market's more historic growth rate of eight to 10 percent.
Investors stampeded into U.S. stocks with a vengeance in 1996 with the Dow industrials surging 27 percent -- well beyond the six to 15 percent predicted by several strategists.

Key factors for 1997 include watching for a marked pickup in world economies that might spur higher interest rates and lower stock prices, and slowing U.S. corporate earnings growth. Wall Street strategists and economists see S&P 500 operating earnings growing only by a consensus of six percent in 1997, down from the seven- eight percent growth seen in 1996, according to First Call.

"The market is high and highly valued. You have to pick well -- it's not like the early and mid-80s. You also have to be sensitive on earnings," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney.

By a few historical measures, a bear market may be due. Since 1950, the stock market has gained 30 percent or more in three years -- 1954, 1958 and 1975. Each of those years was followed by a year in which gains were halved, and then a bear market.
The S&P 500 jumped 38 percent in 1995 and is up 22 percent so far this year.
As a double whammy, the years following presidential re-elections have also proven unfavorable for Wall Street -- down years, if not the start of outright bear markets.
In any case, some analysts suggest the bull run may be ripe for a setback of at least 10 percent -- something not seen in the Dow and S&P 500 in the past six years on a closing basis.
A few analysts were reluctant to pinpoint Dow targets, mindful that the Dow ran roughshod over 1995 and 1996 forecasts.

Many said the staggering amount of money flowing into stock mutual funds had proved to be overwhelming to fundamental measures, and few see the flow withering in 1997 as long as interest rates and the economic climate remain favorable.

"I don't know why we can't sustain a relatively high level (of fund flow). The demographic forces (of aging babyboomers) are pretty powerful. The key is if fundamentals disrupt it -- for example higher interest rates," Acuff said.
Gail Dudack, chief investment strategist at UBS Securities, said volatility has characterized the month of December so far, "and in our view, volatility is here to stay."
Stocks have gyrated since Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan on December 5 posed the rhetorical question of whether there was "irrational exuberance" in stock and other markets.

Among the few in the bear camp is Morgan Stanley's global strategist Barton Biggs. "I think that in 1997 we will experience a true bear market in U.S. stocks ... with a decline of 20 percent to 30 percent peak to trough that will last six months," he said.

Merrill Lynch remains bullish on bonds. "Our economic momentum index indicates that the economy is increasingly threatened by weak demand and lower profits. We think the economic numbers in 1997 will continue to reflect further weakness," chief investment strategist Charles Clough said.
Michael Metz, Oppenheimer and Co's chief investment strategist, predicts 1997 "will be the year indexing fails and you have to be an astute sector selector."

"I think the market goes lower," Metz said. "Whether it's big enough for a bear market I don't know." He set no 1997 Dow target, as his 1996 target of 4860 fell far short of the Dow's current 6500 level. "The big stocks will probably have things going against them. The dollar works against them, valuations are more extended, and portfolio managers are rotating to mid- and small-caps," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker, who sees the Dow in a 6000-6550 range.

As for sectors, Jeffrey Applegate, chief investment strategist at Lehman Brothers, said, "I would still recommend an overweighting in technology, capital goods and financial. Areas to still avoid are basic materials, consumer cyclicals, communication services, utilities and consumer staples."
David Shulman, chief equity strategist at Salomon Brothers, who had a 1996 S&P 500 range of 640-540, sees the S&P ending 1997 at 675, down from 748 Monday at midday.

"S&P 500 P/E's are trading at 19 times this year's earnings. Whenever it's been over 18, the market has had problems," Shulman said. "Our economists see higher rates so at best we see a sideways market next year or, at worst, down 10-15 percent. A correction, not a bear market."

Joseph Barthel, chief investment strategist at Fahnestock & Co, said, "Despite the somewhat muted feelings of 1997 being a good year, what with the first year of a re-elected president and poison pills delivered to the economy, I think monetary policy will be very favorable in 1997."
He added, "Most people are not expecting a lot of disappointment, but there is a 'one foot toward the exit door' sense. Until that becomes 'no one is looking for an exit,' I'm not concerned."
-- Wall Street Desk 212 859 1721
